I don't agree with the headline here. Salon is being sensationalist (of course) and Sotomayor's dissent is so chock full of liberal drama and progressive talking points as to be embarrassing for a high court judge to be associated with.

The case in question had an officer stopping a man after he left a house under surveillance for reported drug activity. running his ID and coming back with a traffic warrant. At that point (being detained for a warrant) the officer searched him, and found drugs and arrested him for possession of a controlled substance.

The defense argued that since the police officer had "no reasonable suspicion of a crime" to stop him initially, that the subsequent discover of a warrant was irrelevant, and the drugs found on his person should not be counted as evidence against him.

But here's where I have issues with this. Utah has a "Stop and Identify" statue that's been on the books for 26 years. (which has been upheld by the supreme court, along with 23 other similar state laws). the actual text of the statute is:

77-7-15. Authority of peace officer to stop and question suspect -- Grounds. A peace officer may stop any person in a public place when he has a reasonable suspicion to believe he has committed or is in the act >of committing or is attempting to commit a public offense and may demand his name, address and an explanation of his actions.

Stopping a guy you think is in violation of the law, getting his ID and running it through the system is 100% legal. Detaining someone with a warrant is 100% legal. Searching someone you've detained is nuanced, but officer safety exceptions generally should have allowed for it, and worst case they guy would be searched when taken to holding/processing. So if the officer had a suspicion that the gentleman in question may be in violation of the law, then everything he did, and the subsequent search and discovery, are fine.

The entire case boils down to: Is it reasonable for a police officer to assume someone coming out of a property under surveillance for illegal activity may be involved in said activity? Honestly I think it is, and apparently so do the majority of the supreme court justices. The defendant in this case was, at all points, in violation of the law. He had outstanding warrants, illegal narcotics, etc. This isn't a case of a good guy wronged by the system, no matter how much sotomayor cries about it.

Anonymous tips are by definition hearsay. Hearsay is not probable cause for a search. "Probable Cause" is not the standard of evidence that lead to the search in this case. "Reasonable suspicion" is. A first year law student would know the difference.
